questions.q: Acharya Kanada said that if matter (dravya) is divided again and again, a stage is reached where the particles can no longer be divided. What did he call these smallest particles?
questions.a: Parmanus: Kanada's name for the smallest particles of matter that cannot be divided further.

questions.q: In which year did John Dalton propose his atomic theory, based on the scientific experiments of his time?
Leucippus and Democritus in ancient Greece called the smallest particles of matter atomos. How did this idea of the atom first arise?
questions.a: As an imagined idea, without experiments: the chapter says the concept of the atom began as an imaginary idea rather than from experimental observations.
o: As an imagined idea, without experiments
From experiments with electric current in gases
From weighing elements in a laboratory
From viewing matter through a microscope

questions.q:
Read the statements about early ideas of the atom.
I. In Kanada's idea, a triad is a group of three parmanus.
II. Kanada's description states the proportions in which parmanus combine to form different substances.
III. Dalton described atoms as the fundamental building blocks of matter that cannot be broken down into smaller parts.
Which of these statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the chapter says Kanada's description does not specify the proportions in which parmanus combine to form different substances.

questions.q:
(a) What does the Greek word atomos mean?
(b) In which Sanskrit text are Acharya Kanada's ideas about parmanus recorded?
questions.a: (a) Atomos means indivisible. (b) The Vaisesika Sutras.
s: (a) States that atomos means indivisible
(b) Names the Vaisesika Sutras

questions.q: True or False: Kanada's parmanu and Dalton's atom were both ideas that came from experiments. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.a: False. Kanada's parmanu, like the Greek atomos, was an imagined (philosophical) idea and not based on experiments; only Dalton's 1808 theory was based on the scientific experiments of his time.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: Kanada's idea was imagined; only Dalton's theory was based on experiments

questions.q:
Answer each part in one line.
(a) According to Kanada, what happens if matter is divided again and again?
(b) What is a dyad?
(c) Can a parmanu be seen or felt with our senses? Give the chapter's reason.
questions.a: (a) We reach the smallest particles, parmanus, which can no longer be divided. (b) A dyad is a group of two parmanus. (c) No; a parmanu is infinitely small and cannot be perceived by the senses.
s: (a) Division ends at parmanus that cannot be divided further
(b) A dyad is a group of two parmanus
(c) No: a parmanu is infinitely small and cannot be perceived

questions.q:
Compare Kanada's parmanu with Dalton's atom.
(a) Give one way in which the two ideas are alike.
(b) Give one way in which they differ in what they were based on.
(c) Using your answer to (b), explain why it is Dalton's theory, and not Kanada's idea, that the chapter calls the first scientific description of how matter is made.
questions.a: (a) Both describe matter as made of the smallest particles that cannot be divided further. (b) Kanada's parmanu was an imagined idea, while Dalton's theory was based on the scientific experiments of his time. (c) A scientific description rests on experimental evidence; Dalton's theory did, so it became the first scientific description and the starting point for later work on atomic structure.
s: (a) Both: smallest indivisible particles of matter
(b) Kanada's was imagined; Dalton's was based on experiments
(c) Dalton's rests on experiments, so it is the first scientific description

questions.q:
Dalton's 1808 theory said that atoms cannot be broken down into smaller parts.
(a) State what Dalton proposed all matter is made of.
(b) Name the phenomenon discovered in the late 19th century, in which certain elements emit invisible energy and particles, and state what it showed about atoms.
(c) Name the particle J. J. Thomson found in 1897 that also showed atoms have smaller parts.
(d) Riya says, 'Atoms were later found to contain smaller particles, so Dalton's theory has no value today.' Using your answers to (a)-(c), state which part of Dalton's idea was shown to be wrong, and decide whether Riya is right, giving one reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) All matter is made of indivisible particles called atoms, the fundamental building blocks of matter. (b) Radioactivity; it showed that atoms must be made of smaller particles, so they are not indivisible. (c) The electron. (d) The evidence in (b) and (c) disproves only the idea that atoms are indivisible. Riya is not right: Dalton's theory, based on the experiments of its time, was the first scientific description of how matter is made and the starting point for today's understanding of atomic structure; early models matter because they show science moving forward one step at a time.
s: (a) All matter is made of indivisible atoms
(b) Radioactivity: showed atoms are made of smaller particles
(c) Names the electron
(d) Indivisibility disproved by (b)/(c); Riya wrong, with a reason (first scientific description / starting point)

questions.q: In J. J. Thomson's 1897 experiment with a glass tube at very low gas pressure, in which direction did the cathode rays move?
questions.a: From the cathode (the negative electrode) to the anode (the positive electrode).
o: From the cathode to the anode
From the anode to the cathode
From the gas to the glass wall
From the vacuum pump to the cathode

questions.q: Thomson's model of the atom is often pictured as a watermelon. In this picture, what do the seeds stand for?
questions.a: Electrons: the seeds are the electrons spread through the atom, and the red pulp is the positively charged matter.

questions.q:
Match each term in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Cathode rays; 2. Alpha particles; 3. Scattering; 4. Plum pudding model.
Column II: (a) the deflection of particles from their straight path; (b) streams of negatively charged particles; (c) a sphere of positive charge with electrons spread through it; (d) tiny positively charged particles emitted from certain radioactive elements.
questions.a: 1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c: cathode rays are streams of negatively charged particles, alpha particles are tiny positive particles from radioactive elements, scattering is deflection from the straight path, and the plum pudding model is a positive sphere with electrons spread through it.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Geiger and Marsden expected the alpha particles to pass straight through the gold foil or be deflected only slightly.
Reason (R): In Thomson's model, the positive charge of the atom was spread out evenly.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: because Thomson's model spread the positive charge evenly, no one place in the atom was expected to push an alpha particle strongly.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) What did Thomson conclude cathode rays are made of?
(b) Which observation about cathode rays showed that electrons are present in the atoms of every element?
questions.a: (a) Streams of negatively charged particles (electrons) with a much smaller mass than atoms. (b) The nature of the cathode rays did not depend on the material of the cathode or on the gas filled in the tube, so electrons must be a part of all atoms.
s: (a) Streams of negatively charged particles, much lighter than atoms
(b) Rays were the same whatever the cathode material or gas

questions.q:
The charge of one electron is -1.602 x 10^-19 C, and by convention it is taken as -1. The electrons of a neutral atom together carry a charge of -1.2816 x 10^-18 C.
(a) How many electrons does the atom have?
(b) What is the total charge of its protons in relative units, and what is the overall charge of the atom?
questions.a: (a) (-1.2816 x 10^-18 C) / (-1.602 x 10^-19 C) = 8 electrons. (b) The atom is neutral, so it has 8 protons with total charge +8 units; +8 + (-8) = 0, so the overall charge is zero.
s: (a) Divides total charge by one electron's charge: 8 electrons
(b) Protons +8 units; overall charge 0

questions.q:
Answer these about the gold foil experiment.
(a) In which year was it carried out, and under which scientist did Geiger and Marsden work?
(b) What was aimed at the thin sheet of gold foil?
(c) Why is the experiment also called an alpha-ray scattering experiment?
questions.a: (a) In 1911, under Ernest Rutherford. (b) A narrow beam of alpha particles. (c) Because some alpha particles were deflected from their straight path, and this deflection is called scattering.
s: (a) 1911, under Ernest Rutherford
(b) A narrow beam of alpha particles
(c) Deflection from the straight path is called scattering

questions.q:
When Thomson discovered the electron, he knew two things: electrons are negatively charged, and atoms as a whole are neutral.
(a) What puzzle did these two facts create?
(b) How did Thomson's model solve this puzzle?
(c) The model was later replaced. Give the reason the chapter still calls it an important step.
questions.a: (a) If atoms contain negative electrons but are neutral, there must be positive charge somewhere in the atom, and it was not known where. (b) He pictured the atom as a sphere of positive charge with electrons spread throughout it, so the charges balance. (c) It was the first genuine attempt to describe how the atom's positive and negative charges stay balanced.
s: (a) Where is the positive charge that balances the electrons?
(b) A positive sphere with electrons spread through it
(c) First genuine attempt to explain how the charges stay balanced

questions.q:
A teacher in Kochi asks two groups to predict the gold foil result before she tells them the real one. Group P uses Thomson's model. Group Q says, 'The atom's positive charge is packed into one very small place.'
(i) What would Group P predict for alpha particles fired at thin gold foil, and why?
(ii) What was actually observed in the experiment?
(iii) Which group's idea fits the real result better? Give one reason.
(iv) Which observation could Thomson's model not explain at all? Explain why an evenly spread positive charge cannot account for it.
questions.a: (i) Group P would predict that the alpha particles pass straight through or are deflected only slightly, because in Thomson's model the positive charge is spread out evenly. (ii) Most alpha particles passed through undeflected, some were sharply deflected and a few even bounced back. (iii) Group Q: a positive charge packed into a tiny place can deflect a positive alpha particle sharply, while most particles that miss it pass straight through. (iv) The large-angle deflections, including the few that bounced back; when the positive charge is spread evenly it is weak in any one place, so it could only bend the positive alpha particles slightly and could never turn them sharply or send them back.
s: (i) Straight through or slight deflection, as positive charge is evenly spread
(ii) Most undeflected, some sharply deflected, a few bounced back
(iii) Group Q, with a reason linking concentrated charge to sharp deflection
(iv) Names large-angle deflection or bouncing back as unexplained
(iv) Explains that spread-out charge can only cause slight deflection

questions.q: Rutherford found that the nucleus is extremely small compared with the whole atom. About how many times smaller than the atom is the nucleus?
questions.a: About 10^5 (one lakh) times: the atom is about 10^-10 m across and the nucleus about 10^-15 m.

questions.q: In the gold foil experiment, most alpha particles passed through the foil without any deflection. What did Rutherford conclude from this?
questions.a: Most of an atom is empty space.
o: Most of an atom is empty space
The atom is a solid, indivisible ball

questions.q: Why is Rutherford's model of the atom called the planetary model?
questions.a: Because the electrons revolve around the nucleus, somewhat like planets orbiting the Sun.
o: Electrons revolve around the nucleus like planets around the Sun
The nucleus revolves around the electrons like the Earth around the Sun
Electrons are spread through the atom like seeds in a fruit
The atom is round and spins on its own axis like a planet

questions.q: Sameer draws an atom whose nucleus holds 13 protons, but by mistake he draws only 10 electrons around it. What is the overall charge of his drawing, and what must he change to show a real atom of this element?
questions.a: +3 units, and he must add 3 electrons: 13 protons give +13 and 10 electrons give -10, so the drawing shows +3; a real atom is neutral, so it needs 13 electrons, 3 more than he drew.
o: 0; no change is needed, as every drawing of an atom is neutral

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Rutherford's model could not explain why atoms are stable.
Reason (R): The nucleus of an atom contains all of its positive charge and most of its mass.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The failure came from the orbiting electron, which is accelerating and so should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus; the nucleus holding the charge and mass does not explain that.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False: In Rutherford's model, an electron going round the nucleus in a circle is accelerating all the time. Give the reason the chapter gives.
questions.a: True. A particle moving in a circular path is constantly changing its direction, and a change of direction means it is accelerating.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: motion in a circle constantly changes direction, which is acceleration

questions.q:
(a) What name did Rutherford give to the particles that give the nucleus its positive charge?
(b) How do these particles compare with electrons in mass and in charge?
questions.a: (a) Protons. (b) Protons are much heavier than electrons, and their charge is equal in size and opposite in sign to that of electrons.
s: (a) Protons
(b) Much heavier; equal and opposite charge

questions.q:
Take the diameter of an atom as about 10^-10 m and that of its nucleus as about 10^-15 m.
(a) Show that the atom is about 10^5 times wider than its nucleus.
(b) Where in the atom are all of its positive charge and most of its mass found?
(c) Use the size comparison in (a) to explain why most alpha particles passed through the gold foil undeflected.
questions.a: (a) 10^-10 m / 10^-15 m = 10^5. (b) In the tiny, dense nucleus at the centre. (c) The nucleus takes up only a tiny part of the atom and the rest is mostly empty space, so most alpha particles never come close to a nucleus and go straight through.
s: (b) In the small, dense nucleus
(c) Most of the atom is empty space, so most particles miss the nucleus

questions.q:
Riya's science club in Lucknow is making a wall display of the Rutherford model. They prepare three atom drawings. Drawing P: a nucleus with charge +8 units and 8 electrons orbiting it. Drawing Q: a nucleus with charge +11 units and 10 electrons orbiting it. Drawing R: a nucleus with charge +2 units and 2 electrons, with the nucleus drawn half as wide as the whole atom.
(a) Which of the drawings show a neutral atom?
(b) What is the overall charge shown in Drawing Q?
(c) What is wrong with the size of the nucleus in Drawing R, according to Rutherford's findings?
(d) A member suggests adding a fourth drawing showing an electron spiralling into the nucleus, 'because that is what Rutherford's model predicts happens to real atoms.' Should the club add it as a picture of real atoms? Decide, giving a reason.
questions.a: (a) Drawings P and R, since in each the positive charge of the nucleus equals the number of electrons. (b) +11 - 10 = +1 unit. (c) Rutherford found the nucleus is about 10^5 (one lakh) times smaller than the atom, so it should be a tiny dot at the centre, not half the atom's width. (d) Not as a picture of real atoms: the model does predict that an accelerating electron loses energy and spirals into the nucleus, but real atoms are stable and matter stays intact. The drawing can be shown only if it is labelled as the limitation of Rutherford's model.
s: (a) P and R are neutral
(b) Q shows +1 unit
(c) Nucleus should be about 10^5 times smaller than the atom
(d) Not real atoms: real atoms are stable; show it only as the model's limitation

questions.q: In Bohr's model of the atom, which shell is closest to the nucleus and has the least energy?
questions.a: The K-shell (n = 1).

questions.q: Who discovered the neutron, and in which year?
questions.a: James Chadwick, in 1932.

questions.q:
Read the statements about Bohr's model of the atom.
I. While moving in a fixed shell, an electron does not lose energy.
II. An electron moves to another shell by absorbing or releasing a fixed amount of energy equal to the difference between the energies of the two levels.
III. An electron in the L-shell has less energy than an electron in the K-shell.
Which of these statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: energy increases away from the nucleus, so an L-shell electron has more energy than a K-shell electron.

questions.q:
(a) How does the mass of a neutron compare with the mass of a proton, and how do their charges differ?
(b) Name the one kind of atom whose nucleus has no neutron.
questions.a: (a) A neutron's mass is nearly equal to a proton's; a proton has a charge of +1 while a neutron has no electrical charge. (b) The hydrogen atom.
s: (a) Nearly equal masses; proton +1, neutron no charge
(b) Hydrogen

questions.q:
In an atom, an electron moves from the L-shell to the K-shell.
(a) Does the electron absorb energy or release energy? Give a reason.
(b) How much energy is involved in this change, in terms of the two shells?
questions.a: (a) It releases energy, because the K-shell is closer to the nucleus and has less energy than the L-shell. (b) A fixed amount equal to the difference between the energies of the L-shell and the K-shell.
s: (a) Releases energy, as K has less energy than L
(b) Amount equals the difference between the L and K energies

questions.q:
Before the neutron was known, scientists counted only protons in the nucleus. A hydrogen atom has 1 proton and no neutron. A helium atom has 2 protons and 2 neutrons. A lithium atom has 3 protons and 4 neutrons. Ignore the mass of electrons.
(a) Counting protons only, how many times as heavy as a hydrogen atom should a helium atom be?
(b) A helium atom is actually about four times as heavy as a hydrogen atom. Explain the difference.
(c) Counting protons only, how many times as heavy as hydrogen should lithium be, and about how many times as heavy is it once its neutrons are counted?
questions.a: (a) 2 times, since it has 2 protons. (b) Helium also has 2 neutrons, each with a mass nearly equal to a proton's, so its mass is about 2 + 2 = 4 times that of hydrogen. (c) Protons only: 3 times; with its 4 neutrons: about 3 + 4 = 7 times.
s: (a) 2 times
(b) The 2 neutrons add mass nearly equal to 2 protons, giving about 4
(c) 3 times from protons; about 7 times with neutrons

questions.q:
A student writes in her notebook: 'Bohr kept Rutherford's nucleus but changed the rules for the electrons.'
(i) Name one feature of Rutherford's model that Bohr kept.
(ii) State what Bohr said about the paths in which electrons move.
(iii) Why, according to Bohr, does an electron not lose energy while it moves round the nucleus?
(iv) Explain how this solves the problem that Rutherford's model could not.
(v) State what must happen for an electron in the K-shell to move to the L-shell.
questions.a: (i) A small positively charged nucleus with electrons moving in circular paths around it. (ii) Electrons move only in fixed circular paths called shells, orbits, stationary states or energy levels, and not in between them. (iii) Bohr introduced stationary states as a postulate: in a stationary state the energy of the electron stays constant even though it is moving. (iv) In Rutherford's model the orbiting electron should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, so atoms would collapse; in Bohr's model it keeps its energy, so the atom stays stable. (v) It must absorb a fixed amount of energy equal to the difference between the energies of the L and K shells.
s: (i) Names a feature kept: nucleus with electrons moving around it
(ii) Fixed shells (energy levels), not in between
(iii) Stationary states: energy stays constant
(iv) Links constant energy to no spiralling, so the atom is stable
(v) Absorbs energy equal to the L minus K difference

questions.q:
Two students explain why heavy atoms have many more neutrons than protons in their nucleus. Arun says, 'Neutrons carry negative charge, so they cancel the positive charge of the protons.' Bina says, 'Neutrons are neutral; they reduce the repulsion between protons by sitting between them, and they strengthen the force that binds the nucleus.'
(a) Why do the protons in a nucleus push each other away?
(b) Evaluate Arun's explanation.
(c) Evaluate Bina's explanation.
(d) A uranium nucleus has 92 protons and 146 neutrons. How many more neutrons than protons does it have?
questions.a: (a) All protons carry positive charge, and like charges repel, so every proton repels every other proton. (b) Arun is wrong: a neutron has no electrical charge (relative charge 0), so it cannot cancel any charge. (c) Bina is right: neutral neutrons increase the distance between protons, which reduces their repulsion, and they strengthen the nuclear force that binds the particles together, so heavier nuclei need more neutrons. (d) 146 - 92 = 54 more neutrons.
s: (a) Protons are all positive, and like charges repel
(b) Arun wrong: neutrons have no charge
(c) Bina right: neutrons space out protons and strengthen the nuclear force
(d) 54 more neutrons

questions.q: The symbol of iron is Fe. From which name does this symbol come?
questions.a: From the Latin name ferrum.

questions.q: Four students write the symbol of magnesium on the board. Which one follows the IUPAC norm for writing symbols?
questions.a: Mg: the first letter is a capital and the second letter is a small letter.

questions.q: The nucleus of an atom has 8 protons and 9 neutrons. What is the mass number of this atom?
questions.a: 17, because mass number = protons + neutrons = 8 + 9.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The symbol of zinc is Zn.
Reason (R): The symbol of every element is made of the first two letters of its English name.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. Zn is correct, but not every symbol uses the first two letters: chlorine is Cl and zinc is Zn, and some symbols, like Fe for iron, come from Latin, Greek or German names.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) Define the atomic number of an element and give the letter used for it.
(b) A neutral atom has atomic number 7. How many electrons does it have?
questions.a: (a) The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom of the element; it is written Z. (b) 7 electrons, because in a neutral atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
s: (a) Number of protons in the nucleus; symbol Z
(b) 7 electrons, equal to the protons

questions.q:
A neutral atom of neon (Ne) has 10 electrons and 10 neutrons.
(a) Find its atomic number and mass number.
(b) Describe how this atom is written in standard notation: which number goes above, which goes below, and where they are placed.
questions.a: (a) Atomic number = 10 (protons = electrons in a neutral atom); mass number = 10 + 10 = 20. (b) The mass number 20 is written above and the atomic number 10 below, both on the left of the symbol Ne.
s: (a) Z = 10 and A = 20
(b) 20 above, 10 below, before the symbol Ne

questions.q:
Imran says, 'An atom with 11 protons and 12 neutrons, and another atom with 12 protons and 11 neutrons, are atoms of the same element because both have the same mass number.'
(a) Find the mass number of each atom.
(b) Find the atomic number of each atom.
(c) Is Imran right? Explain which number decides the identity of an element.
questions.a: (a) 11 + 12 = 23 and 12 + 11 = 23, so both have mass number 23. (b) The atomic numbers are 11 and 12. (c) Imran is wrong: the atomic number (number of protons) determines the identity of an element, so the first is sodium (Z = 11) and the second is magnesium (Z = 12), two different elements.
s: (a) Both mass numbers are 23
(b) Atomic numbers 11 and 12
(c) Wrong: atomic number decides identity, so they are different elements

questions.q:
At a science fair in Guwahati, Class 9 students run an 'atom card' stall. Each card shows only the nucleus of a neutral atom, and visitors must work out the rest. Card 1: 3 protons and 4 neutrons. Card 2: 6 protons and 6 neutrons. Card 3: 9 protons and 10 neutrons. The symbols to be matched to the cards are C, F and Li.
(a) How many electrons does the atom on Card 1 have?
(b) What is the mass number of the atom on Card 2?
(c) What are the atomic number and the mass number of the atom on Card 3?
(d) Which symbol goes with each card?
questions.a: (a) 3 electrons, equal to its 3 protons. (b) 6 + 6 = 12. (c) Atomic number 9; mass number 9 + 10 = 19. (d) Card 1 (Z = 3) is lithium, Li; Card 2 (Z = 6) is carbon, C; Card 3 (Z = 9) is fluorine, F.
s: (a) 3 electrons
(b) Mass number 12
(c) Z = 9 and A = 19
(d) Card 1 Li, Card 2 C, Card 3 F

questions.q:
Meera is making a wall chart that sorts the symbols of elements by the IUPAC norm each one follows.
(a) Write the symbol of nitrogen, which is just the first letter of its name.
(b) Write the symbol of argon, which uses the first two letters of its name, with the correct capital and small letter.
(c) Write the symbol of silver and name the Latin word it comes from.
(d) Give one reason why scientists everywhere use these symbols instead of the names of elements in their own languages.
questions.a: (a) N. (b) Ar: capital A followed by small r. (c) Ag, from the Latin name Argentum. (d) The symbols are recognised internationally, so scientists all over the world can communicate clearly whatever language they speak.
s: (a) N
(b) Ar, with capital A and small r
(c) Ag, from Argentum
(d) Internationally recognised, so clear communication across languages

questions.q: Using the rule 2n^2, what is the largest number of electrons the M-shell (n = 3) can hold?
What is the electronic configuration of a nitrogen atom (atomic number 7)?
questions.a: 2, 5: two electrons fill the K-shell and the remaining five go into the L-shell.

questions.q:
Match each element in Column I with its valency in Column II.
Column I: 1. Magnesium (2, 8, 2); 2. Nitrogen (2, 5); 3. Fluorine (2, 7); 4. Silicon (2, 8, 4).
Column II: (a) 1; (b) 2; (c) 3; (d) 4.
questions.a: 1-b, 2-c, 3-a, 4-d: magnesium loses 2 electrons (valency 2), nitrogen gains 8 - 5 = 3, fluorine gains 8 - 7 = 1, and silicon, with 4 valence electrons, shares 4.

questions.q:
(a) What is meant by the valence shell of an atom?
(b) How many valence electrons does an atom with the configuration 2, 8, 3 have?
questions.a: (a) The valence shell is the outermost shell of an atom that contains electrons. (b) 3 valence electrons, the electrons in its outermost (M) shell.
s: (a) The outermost shell that contains electrons
(b) 3 valence electrons

questions.q:
(a) Write the electronic configuration of boron (atomic number 5) and state its valency.
(b) Using your answer to (a), how many chlorine atoms will one boron atom combine with?
questions.a: (a) 2, 3; it has 3 valence electrons, fewer than four, so it tends to lose them: valency 3. (b) 3 chlorine atoms, because chlorine has a combining capacity of one and boron's combining capacity is 3.
s: (a) Configuration 2, 3 and valency 3
(b) Combines with 3 chlorine atoms

questions.q:
Answer these using the Bohr-Bury rules.
(a) Use 2n^2 to show that the L-shell (n = 2) can hold 8 electrons.
(b) What is the largest number of electrons an atom's outermost shell can hold, if it has more than one shell?
(c) In which shell does filling begin, and which shell is filled next?
questions.a: (a) 2 x 2^2 = 2 x 4 = 8. (b) 8 electrons. (c) Filling begins in the K-shell, closest to the nucleus; the L-shell is filled next, only after the K-shell is complete.
s: (b) 8 electrons in the outermost shell
(c) K first, then L after K is complete

questions.q:
Two students write the electronic configuration of chlorine (atomic number 17). Rekha writes 2, 15. Arjun writes 2, 7, 8.
(a) Which Bohr-Bury rules does Rekha's answer break?
(b) Which rule does Arjun's answer break?
(c) Write the correct configuration and find chlorine's valency.
questions.a: (a) The L-shell can hold at most 2 x 2^2 = 8 electrons, and the outermost shell can hold at most 8, so 15 in the L-shell breaks both rules. (b) Shells fill stepwise: the M-shell can start only after the L-shell is complete, but Arjun puts electrons in M while L has only 7. (c) 2, 8, 7; with 7 valence electrons (more than four) it gains 1 electron, so its valency is 8 - 7 = 1.
s: (a) Rekha: more than 8 in L and in the outermost shell
(b) Arjun: M started before L was complete
(c) 2, 8, 7 and valency 1

questions.q:
Consider three atoms: lithium (atomic number 3), oxygen (atomic number 8) and neon (atomic number 10).
(i) Write the electronic configuration of each.
(ii) Write the number of valence electrons in each.
(iii) Say whether each atom tends to lose electrons, gain electrons, or neither.
(iv) Write the valency of lithium and of oxygen.
(v) Why is neon largely unreactive?
questions.a: (i) Lithium 2, 1; oxygen 2, 6; neon 2, 8. (ii) 1, 6 and 8. (iii) Lithium tends to lose its 1 electron, oxygen tends to gain 2 electrons, and neon neither loses nor gains. (iv) Lithium 1; oxygen 8 - 6 = 2. (v) Neon has a complete octet (8 electrons) in its valence shell, which is stable.
s: (ii) Valence electrons 1, 6 and 8
(iii) Li loses, O gains, Ne neither
(iv) Valency Li 1, O 2
(v) Neon has a complete octet, so it is stable

questions.q:
A chemistry club in Indore has four sample cards. Each shows the formula of a compound of an element with hydrogen or chlorine, and the electronic configuration of that element. Card W: CH4, carbon 2, 4. Card X: AlCl3, aluminium 2, 8, 3. Card Y: H2S, sulfur 2, 8, 6. Card Z: NaCl, sodium 2, 8, 1. Hydrogen and chlorine each have a combining capacity of one.
(a) From the formulas, find the valency of carbon, aluminium, sulfur and sodium.
(b) Check whether the valency worked out from each configuration agrees with your answers in (a).
(c) Which of the four elements tends to share electrons rather than lose or gain them?
(d) A member writes on the board: 'Sulfur's valency is 6 because it has 6 valence electrons.' Should the club accept this? Decide using the data.
questions.a: (a) Carbon 4, aluminium 3, sulfur 2, sodium 1 (the number of H or Cl atoms each combines with). (b) They agree: carbon has 4 valence electrons and shares 4 (valency 4); aluminium has 3 and loses them (3); sulfur has 6 and gains 8 - 6 = 2 (2); sodium has 1 and loses it (1). (c) Carbon, with exactly four valence electrons. (d) No: an atom with more than four valence electrons tends to gain electrons to complete its octet, so sulfur's valency is 8 - 6 = 2, which matches H2S, where one sulfur atom combines with two hydrogen atoms.
s: (a) C 4, Al 3, S 2, Na 1
(b) Configurations give the same valencies
(c) Carbon shares
(d) Reject: S gains 2, valency 2, matching H2S

questions.q: Naturally occurring hydrogen is a mixture of three isotopes. Which of them has no neutron in its nucleus?
questions.a: Protium: it has one proton and no neutron, while deuterium has one neutron and tritium has two.
o: None of them; all three have one neutron

questions.q: Which isotope is used in archaeology and geology to find the age of ancient fossils and artefacts?
questions.a: Carbon-14.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
I. Deuterium has two neutrons in its nucleus.
II. Each of the three isotopes of carbon has six electrons.
III. Isobars are atoms of different elements with the same mass number but different atomic numbers.
Which of these statements are correct?
questions.a: II and III only. Statement I is wrong: deuterium has one neutron; it is tritium that has two.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Protium and deuterium are atoms of two different elements, because their mass numbers are different.
Reason (R): Deuterium has one neutron in its nucleus, while protium has none.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. Both have one proton (atomic number 1), so both are hydrogen; they are isotopes, which differ only in their number of neutrons.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
(a) Define isotopes.
(b) Write the mass numbers of the three isotopes of carbon.
questions.a: (a) Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers. (b) 12, 13 and 14 (carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14).
s: (a) Same atomic number, different mass numbers

questions.q: True or False: The simple arithmetic mean of the masses of an element's isotopes always gives its correct average atomic mass. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. Isotopes do not occur in equal amounts, so the average must be weighted by each isotope's abundance; for chlorine the simple average is 36 u, but the weighted average is 35.5 u.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: isotopes occur in unequal amounts, so a weighted average is needed

questions.q:
A hypothetical element has two isotopes: one of mass 20 u making up 90% of its atoms, and one of mass 22 u making up 10%.
(a) Find the simple arithmetic mean of the two isotope masses.
(b) Find the weighted average atomic mass of the element.
(c) Explain why the weighted average is much closer to 20 u than the simple mean is.
questions.a: (a) (20 + 22) / 2 = 21 u. (b) 20 x 90/100 + 22 x 10/100 = 18 + 2.2 = 20.2 u. (c) The 20 u isotope makes up 90% of the atoms, so it counts far more in the weighted average; the simple mean treats both isotopes as equally common, which they are not.
s: (a) Simple mean 21 u
(b) Weighted average 20.2 u
(c) The 90% isotope dominates; the simple mean ignores abundance

questions.q:
Four atoms are described by the particles in their nuclei. Atom P: 6 protons, 7 neutrons. Atom Q: 7 protons, 6 neutrons. Atom R: 6 protons, 6 neutrons. Atom S: 5 protons, 8 neutrons.
(i) Find the mass number of each atom.
(ii) Name the element each atom belongs to, using the atomic numbers boron 5, carbon 6 and nitrogen 7.
(iii) Which two atoms are isotopes? Give a reason.
(iv) Which atoms are isobars of one another? Give a reason.
(v) Which two atoms will have the same chemical properties, and why?
questions.a: (i) P 13, Q 13, R 12, S 13. (ii) P carbon, Q nitrogen, R carbon, S boron. (iii) P and R: same atomic number (6) but different mass numbers (13 and 12). (iv) P, Q and S: they are different elements (atomic numbers 6, 7 and 5) with the same mass number, 13. (v) P and R, because isotopes have the same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration, and chemical properties depend mainly on the valence electrons.
s: (i) Mass numbers 13, 13, 12, 13
(ii) P carbon, Q nitrogen, R carbon, S boron
(iii) P and R are isotopes: same Z, different A
(iv) P, Q and S are isobars: different Z, same A of 13
(v) P and R: same electronic configuration, so same chemical properties

questions.q:
A school lab in Hyderabad studies two samples of a hypothetical element, Vidium, collected from two places. Every Vidium atom has the same atomic number, but each atom has a mass of either 50 u or 52 u. Sample A contains 1000 atoms: 600 of mass 50 u and 400 of mass 52 u. Sample B contains 1000 atoms: 900 of mass 50 u and 100 of mass 52 u.
(a) What percentage of the atoms in Sample A have a mass of 52 u?
(b) Find the weighted average atomic mass of Vidium in Sample A.
(c) Find the weighted average atomic mass of Vidium in Sample B.
(d) A student concludes, 'The two samples must be two different elements, because their average atomic masses are different.' Should the lab accept this? Decide, giving a reason.
questions.a: (a) 400/1000 x 100 = 40%. (b) 50 x 60/100 + 52 x 40/100 = 30 + 20.8 = 50.8 u. (c) 50 x 90/100 + 52 x 10/100 = 45 + 5.2 = 50.2 u. (d) No: all the atoms have the same atomic number, so both samples are the same element; the 50 u and 52 u atoms are isotopes, and the averages differ only because the two isotopes are present in different proportions.
s: (d) Reject: same atomic number, so same element; only isotope proportions differ
